analysis.one_liner: Lets states, cities, and gun-violence victims sue gun makers, dealers, and importers for the costs of gun violence.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have opened gun makers and sellers to federal lawsuits over gun violence, never got a committee or floor vote and died in the Senate Judiciary Committee at the end of the 106th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have created a new federal right to sue firearms manufacturers, dealers, and importers in federal or state court. Anyone hurt by gun violence, or stuck with its bills—states, cities, businesses, organizations—could sue a company that knew, or should have known, that its design, manufacturing, marketing, or sales practices would likely lead to gun violence. Courts could award actual damages, punitive damages, and attorneys' fees. The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee and never received any further action.
analysis.who_benefits: States, cities, victims of gun violence, businesses, and organizations that bear the costs of shootings—police, emergency care, lost life and productivity—would gain a federal legal tool to recover those costs from gun makers, dealers, and importers whose practices likely fed the violence. Courts could also award punitive damages and cover litigation costs, including expert witnesses.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a federal cause of action letting states, local governments, organizations, businesses, and other persons injured by or burdened with the costs of gun violence sue manufacturers, dealers, or importers whose practices would likely result in gun violence [S2][S3].
Allows courts to award actual damages, punitive damages, attorneys' fees, and litigation costs including expert witnesses, shifting the public costs of gun violence onto the industry [S2][S3].

The bill states Congress's finding that the costs of gun violence—law enforcement, medical care, lost productivity, loss of life—should be borne by those liable for them, including manufacturers, dealers, and importers [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Firearms manufacturers, dealers, and importers would bear the cost: exposure to federal lawsuits and potentially large damages judgments for design, marketing, and distribution practices linked to gun violence. Gun dealers in particular would face suits over how and to whom they sold weapons.

drawbacks.text: The standard is broad: a manufacturer, dealer, or importer can be sued if it 'knew or reasonably should have known' its sales, marketing, or distribution practices would likely result in gun violence [S2][S3]. Critics would argue this could expose lawful sellers to liability for criminal acts committed far downstream of their transactions.

The bill applies 'notwithstanding' any federal, state, or local law [S3], so it would override existing state liability rules nationwide—an honest supporter would acknowledge this raises federalism concerns and invites years of litigation over what practices 'likely result' in violence.
Heavy litigation exposure could impose real costs on small dealers and push some out of business, and juries' punitive damages awards could be unpredictable.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would shift the enormous public costs of gun violence—police, medical care, lost lives—from taxpayers and victims onto the industry, and create a financial incentive for safer design and distribution. The costs are real: broad liability standards, litigation burdens that could fall hardest on small dealers, and a federal override of state law. On balance the bill was drafted to make an industry internalize costs it had historically externalized, but its breadth invited legitimate objection.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Barbara Boxer introduced the bill on March 23, 1999, joined by five cosponsors including Republican John Chafee, for a total of six cosponsors (4 Democrats, 2 Republicans) [S3][S4].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day [S1][S5].
No further action—no committee markup, no hearing listed, no floor vote—appears in the bill's action history for the rest of the 106th Congress [S5].
The bill died when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001, without ever receiving a vote in either chamber [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Firearms manufacturers, dealers, and importers came out ahead: a federal liability regime that would have let governments and victims recover the costs of gun violence from the industry never took effect, and no comparable bill advanced during the Congress.

for.name: Sen. Barbara Boxer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and sponsored it throughout, framing it as a way to make the industry bear the costs of gun violence.

for.name: 6 Senate cosponsors (4 Democrats, 2 Republicans)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Republican Sen. John Chafee of Rhode Island among the original cosponsors named at introduction.

against.name: Senate Committee on the Judiciary
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day of introduction and took no further action on it—no markup, no vote, no report—for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Sen. Orrin Hatch
against.what_they_did: Chaired the Judiciary Committee during the 106th Congress; the committee never scheduled action on the bill, which stalled there until it died.

against.name: National Rifle Association
against.what_they_did: Opposed efforts to open the firearms industry to lawsuits over gun violence during this period, pressuring lawmakers against liability measures like this one.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's support was bipartisan but thin—six cosponsors split 4 Democrats and 2 Republicans—and no votes were ever taken, so the partisan shape of opposition was never recorded.

industries.note: The bill would have exposed the entire gun trade to federal lawsuits and potentially large damages awards for design, marketing, and sales practices linked to gun violence. Its failure left the industry free of that federal liability regime.

industries.industry: Hospitals, emergency care, and local law enforcement
industries.note: These entities absorb much of the cost of gun violence; the bill would have let organizations, businesses, and governments that incurred those costs sue to recover them [S2][S3].
